name: Sam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a response officer at the central station, so city centre: shops, the train station, the bars on Canal Street at weekends. A day shift is shoplifters, people locked out of their cars, the odd assault, and a lot of driving between them. I'm one of the volunteers testing the force's pilot that drafts reports from your body camera footage, which I love, because it means I'm not typing at the end of a twelve-hour shift. The hardest part is still the human bit, like the woman at the train station last week who'd just been told her son had died.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on that pilot, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put my hand up the minute the email came round, because I already use AI for pretty much everything at home, meal plans, my budget, practising for my exams. The drafts are good on simple jobs, like a theft from a shop, and rubbish on anything messy, like a domestic where three people tell three stories. You have to read every line, but it still saves me maybe forty minutes a shift. My sergeant's half impressed and half suspicious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, that'd be a bit of a let-down for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not magic, and we should stop pretending it's either a saviour or a monster. I'd post something like that on the team chat, probably with a screenshot of the report draft that called a bicycle a 'two-wheeled suspect'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing much changes for me, and that's fine. The job's secure, my pay is normal, and my boyfriend Theo and I have about five months saved. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped the tools would free up time for actual policing, but I'd survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the report pilot and push for it to be rolled out to the whole team. I'd keep studying for the cyber crime unit, because computers aren't going away even if AI stalls. And I'd keep being the person who helps the older officers when their tablets freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. It's like being told the new road isn't getting built after all. You shrug and take the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're keen on AI. Is there anything about it in policing that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Facial recognition, definitely. Even a half-working facial recognition system gets pointed at the poorer estates first, and the mistakes land on people who already don't trust us. I'd want an independent board checking where cameras go and how often they're wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Theo say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo tests software for a bank, so he'd be relieved, honestly. His whole job is checking code, and he's been nervous about AI doing that. If AI stalls, his job is safe, and he'd buy a bottle of something nice to celebrate.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, not magic, saviour or monster.
He'd mock the pilot's **funnier mistakes** on the team chat.
think: His **job is secure** and five months of savings feel solid.
He'd be **disappointed** the tools didn't free more policing time.
His partner's **bank job** would be safer, a relief at home.
do: Push to roll the **report pilot** out to his whole team.
Keep studying for the **cyber crime unit**.
Keep helping **older officers** with their tablets.
feel: **Calm**, a little flat and let down.
Relieved for **Theo**, whose job feels safer.
S0.quote: Even a half-working facial recognition system gets pointed at the poorer estates first, and the mistakes land on people who already don't trust us.
fieldNote: An **early adopter** who still names facial recognition as his red line.
His keenness for AI sits alongside a strong **progressive** view of oversight.
Household feels **secure**; mild disappointment is the only cost.

steps.text: Ask his inspector to roll the report pilot out team-wide
Keep studying evenings for the cyber crime unit application
Carry on day shifts on city centre response

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I can actually picture. It's half happening on my team already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to get officers out from behind screens and back onto the street. I'd be the one at the team meeting saying, look, the draft saved me forty minutes, here's how to check it properly. Online I'd be careful, but I'd say it should come with clear rules about privacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The officers who can work with these tools will get the specialist posts, and I'm already one of them. The cyber crime unit will need people who understand both policing and software, and that's exactly my plan. I do worry for Theo, though, because 'checking' is literally his job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the cyber crime unit in the first round, probably next spring. I'd take every AI training the force offers and offer to run sessions for my team. And I'd email the association to back an independent board for facial recognition, so the tech I'm cheering for doesn't get used badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. There's a bit of guilt in it, because Steady Disruption is good for me when it isn't good for everyone. But mostly I'd feel like the thing I've been betting on paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you worry about Theo. What would you two actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down with a laptop and look at what testing jobs are turning into, probably people who check what the AI built rather than writing tests by hand. I'd push Theo to learn that now, not after his bank restructures. We'd hold off on moving to a two-bed until his side looks settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lad two years ahead of me who still writes in a paper notebook and freezes when the tablet updates. He's brilliant with people, better than me. I'd worry the new targets make him look slow when he's actually the one you want at a domestic.

say: AI is a chance to get officers **back onto the street**.
He'd show colleagues how to **check drafts** properly.
think: Officers fluent with the tools will **win specialist posts**.
His plan for the **cyber crime unit** fits this world.
His partner's **testing job** is directly in the firing line.
do: Apply to the **cyber crime unit** in next spring's round.
Take all AI training and **teach his team**.
Email the association backing a **facial recognition board**.
feel: **Excited**, feeling his bet has paid off.
A little **guilty** that it suits him more than others.
S1.quote: There's a bit of guilt in it, because Steady Disruption is good for me when it isn't good for everyone.
fieldNote: He's frank that **disruption suits him**, and uneasy about saying so.
Concern for a **slower colleague** shows he sees unfairness in speed targets.
Household risk sits with **Theo's job**, which he plans around early.

steps.text: Apply to the cyber crime unit next spring
Run short AI drafting sessions for his response team
Email the association to back a facial recognition oversight board
Delay moving to a two-bed until Theo's job settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Wow. That's two years. That's before I'd even be settled in a new unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need a pause on AGI in policing until there's proper law: who's accountable, who checks it, who can appeal. I'd join anything pushing for that, petitions, the association, maybe a party. I'd still say the tech can be good, but not with no brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it flips my whole plan. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, then cyber crime analysis is the first thing it takes, and that was my escape route. Theo's job goes almost straight away, so we'd be on my wage alone. The weird bit is the hands-on part of policing, the doorsteps and the fights, is what lasts longest, until around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the cyber crime application and stay on response, because that's three more years of guaranteed hands-on work. We'd cut back hard: no holiday, cancel the streaming and the car lease, and live on my wage so Theo's redundancy pay goes straight into savings. And I'd make myself the officer who supervises the AI, the one who checks its decisions, because somebody has to sign them off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary, honestly. Not panic, because I've got ideas, but I'd be lying awake doing the maths on one wage. The strange thing is realising the bit of the job I was trying to escape is the bit that keeps me employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031, when robots can do the hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't plan for. My guess is the law will still say a human makes an arrest, so maybe there's a smaller number of us supervising machines on the street. I'd want to be one of those, which means a sergeant's exam by thirty. If not, I'd be looking at a different life entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Theo the night his bank cuts his team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boyfriend Theo it's not his fault, and we're a team, and my wage covers rent. Then I'd make him a coffee and open a spreadsheet, because that's how we both calm down. We'd probably put off any talk of getting married for a year.

He'd join **petitions and the association** to demand it.
The tech can be good, but **not without brakes**.
think: AGI would take **cyber crime analysis**, his planned escape route.
Theo's job would go fast, leaving them on **one wage**.
Hands-on street work now **lasts longest**, until around 2031.

Cut the holiday, streaming and **car lease** to live on one wage.
Become the officer who **checks AI decisions**.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake doing the maths on one income.
Struck by the **irony** that street work now protects him.
S2.quote: The strange thing is realising the bit of the job I was trying to escape is the bit that keeps me employed.
fieldNote: The **thinking-first, robots-later** order flips his plan from desk to street.
Household risk is now **Theo's job** going almost at once.
Adaptive and full of ideas, but the **one-wage maths** keeps him up.

steps.text: Withdraw the cyber crime application and stay on response
Cancel the car lease, streaming and summer holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. That's a better runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so let's start writing the rules now rather than in a panic in 2030. I'd want to be on whatever group the force sets up to plan it, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can work with five years. Theo has time to move from testing into something more hands-on or people-facing, and I've got time to get to sergeant. My bet would be that the officers who manage and check AI and robots are the ones who stay, and I want to be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the sergeant's exam in 2028, earlier than I planned. I'd skip the cyber crime unit because it'd only last a couple of years. And we'd push our savings from five months up to eight, by putting Theo's annual bonus straight in rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. AGI by 2031 is a serious change, but I feel like I'd be steering, not being dragged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Theo move into, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talked about teaching maths, actually, which he'd be great at. With five years he could do the course part-time while still working. I'd cover more of the rent while he trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up to make that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat in the centre, probably. We'd move a bit further out where rent's cheaper, maybe near the tram line, so I can still get to the station for an early shift. It's not a big sacrifice for five years of breathing room.

say: Write **the rules now**, not in a panic in 2030.
He'd volunteer for the force's **planning group** on AI.
think: Five years is a **workable runway** for him and Theo.
Officers who **manage AI and robots** will be the ones who stay.
He aims to reach **sergeant** before the change lands.
do: Sit the **sergeant's exam** in 2028, earlier than planned.
Raise savings from five to **eight months** with Theo's bonus.
feel: **Uneasy**, but feeling in charge of the change.
S3.quote: AGI by 2031 is a serious change, but I feel like I'd be steering, not being dragged.
fieldNote: Household income could still shrink while **Theo retrains**, so this is anxious, not calm.
He thinks in **career moves**, choosing sergeant over a specialist unit.
Willing to **move further out** to fund his partner's training.

steps.text: Put Theo's yearly bonus straight into savings
Move further out near the tram line for cheaper rent
Cover more rent while Theo trains as a maths teacher

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to build a whole career around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to make this good for everyone, and if it isn't, that's on the people in charge. I'd want police and the public deciding together where AI is allowed and where it isn't, and I'd say that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's great for me. I'd do the cyber crime unit after all, get five or six years in, then move into managing AI tools for investigations before 2036. By the time robots arrive around 2039, I'd be in my late thirties with a skill set that's rare. Theo has a decade to land somewhere safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the cyber crime unit next spring as planned. I'd start putting a hundred a month into a low-cost index fund, because if AI makes companies richer I'd like a small slice. And I'd keep learning every tool as it comes, the way I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. There's a worry at the back, because ten years can turn into five if someone gets a breakthrough, so I'd keep the five-year plan in my back pocket. But I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned ten years turning into five. Would you plan for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd keep an eye on the news every year and be ready to switch to the five-year plan, sergeant's exam and all. Having the plans already made is what keeps me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The officers who don't want to learn any of it, like the guy two years ahead of me with the paper notebook. Ten years is plenty, but only if someone actually trains him on paid time. Otherwise he's left behind slowly instead of quickly.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to make AI good for everyone.
Police and the public should **decide together** where AI goes.
think: The change looks **good for him**, with a rare skill set by 2036.
He'd do **cyber crime** first, then manage AI tools.
Theo has **a decade** to find secure work.
do: Apply to the **cyber crime unit** next spring as planned.
Put **a hundred a month** into an index fund.
Keep learning **every new tool** as it arrives.
feel: A small **worry** that ten years could shrink to five.
S4.quote: Ten years can turn into five if someone gets a breakthrough, so I'd keep the five-year plan in my back pocket.
fieldNote: Keeps **backup plans** ready, which is what keeps him calm.
Wants AI's gains **shared**: index fund for himself, paid training for others.
Still worries about **slower colleagues** being left behind quietly.

steps.text: Apply to the cyber crime unit next spring
Put a hundred a month into a low-cost index fund
Learn each new AI investigation tool when it arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes Theo's job and my plan at the same time. What would help is income support for people like Theo while they retrain, and a clear legal line that a human officer is accountable for every decision, so there's a role for people like me supervising.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Everyone talks about what AI can do, but in policing the real question is who chooses where the cameras point and who checks the machine when it's wrong. That should be the public, not a supplier.

headlineQuote: In policing the real question is who chooses where the cameras point and who checks the machine when it's wrong.
portrait: A 27-year-old **city centre** response officer renting with his partner Theo, a bank software tester.
Uses AI daily and volunteers on the force's **report-drafting pilot**; aims for the cyber crime unit.
Progressive: excited by the tools but firm on **oversight** of facial recognition and accountability.
Calm in slow worlds; **alarmed** in the fastest because Theo's job and his own desk plans collapse together.
Keeps **backup plans** ready and turns each timeline into a concrete career move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which ends Theo's job and his own cyber crime plan at once.
whatWouldHelp: A legal rule that a **human officer** is accountable for every decision.
